labels.predictability.high: Spelling is a reliable guide to sound: learn the rules and you can read almost any word aloud.
labels.predictability.medium: Spelling is mostly a guide to sound, but there are silent letters and a few surprises.
labels.predictability.low: Spelling is a poor guide to sound: the same letters can sound different from word to word.
labels.stress.rule_with_written_accents: Stress follows a simple rule, and a written accent marks every exception.
labels.stress.mostly_penultimate: Most words are stressed on the second-to-last syllable. The stress usually isn’t written.
labels.stress.phrase_final: Stress falls on the last syllable of a phrase, so words don’t carry their own stress the way English words do.
labels.stress.marked_on_every_word: Every word of two or more syllables has its stressed vowel marked, so you always see where the stress goes.
labels.stress.unpredictable: Stress changes from word to word and usually isn’t written, so you learn it with each word.
labels.sound.trill: A rolled r: the tongue taps against the ridge behind your teeth several times.
labels.sound.velar_fricative: A breathy sound from the back of the mouth, like a soft clearing of the throat.
labels.sound.silent_letter: A letter that is written but not pronounced.
labels.sound.b_v_same: Written v, but pronounced like b.
labels.sound.nasal_vowel: The vowel is pronounced through the nose. A tilde, or an n or m after the vowel, marks it, and the n or m isn’t pronounced as a separate consonant.
labels.sound.front_rounded_vowel: Say “ee” with your lips rounded as if for “oo”.
labels.sound.uvular_r: An r made at the back of the throat, a bit like a gentle gargle.
labels.sound.liaison: A final consonant that is normally silent is often pronounced before a vowel, as in “les amis”.
labels.sound.guttural_r: At the start of a word this r is made at the back of the throat, close to an English h (in Brazilian Portuguese).
labels.sound.affricate_before_i: In Brazilian Portuguese, d before i sounds like the “j” in “judge”.
labels.sound.hard_c_before_i: Ch is a hard k sound here, not the “ch” of “church”.
labels.sound.double_consonant: A written double consonant is pronounced longer, and it changes the word.
labels.sound.dental_fricative: The tongue touches the teeth, as in “think” or “this”.
labels.sound.voiced_velar_fricative: Like a very soft g, with the air still flowing.
labels.sound.many_spellings_one_sound: Several spellings share one sound, so the same sound can be written more than one way.
labels.sound.approximant_r: The tongue curls back or bunches up without touching anything.
labels.sound.spelling_varies: The same letters can sound completely different in different words.
labels.q.hear_pick: Listen and pick the word you hear.
labels.q.which_spelling: Which spelling makes the sound in this word?
